title: Optimize-via-Estimate: How to Make Finite-Sample Corrections for Sampling Uncertainty in Data-Driven Optimization
authors: Gar Goei Loke; Taozeng Zhu; Ruiting Zuo
affiliations: Durham University Business School, Department of Management and Marketing, Durham, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland; Dongbei University of Finance and Economics, Institute of Supply Chain Analytics, Dalian, China; National University of Singapore, Analytics & Operations, Singapore, Singapore
abstract: We propose a novel procedure for correcting for the effects of sampling and parameter uncertainty in data-driven convex optimization. We consider the data-driven setting wherein the distribution lies in a parametric family with unknown parameter. The decision-maker possesses a historical data set, from which solves a prescriptive solution as a function mapping such a data set to decisions, and measures its out-of-sample performance as an average over data sets of the same size under the sampling distribution. As the parameter is unknown to the decision-maker, we argue that this problem is ill-defined and further prove that there cannot exist solutions generalizably optimal over all parameters. As such, we formulate the problem as a weighted multi-criteria optimization with weights defined by a density (termed ‘prior’) over the uncertain parameter, and call its optimal solution prior optimal. We prove that sufficient conditions for prior optimality reduces to functions of the sufficient statistic of the parametric family, and this function can be solved as a point-wise optima of a corrected function of the original objective, with terms accounting for parameter uncertainty and sampling uncertainty respectively. The correction for sampling interpretation is verified by a close to (but not) zero ex-ante regret against a perfect information oracle in numerical illustrations on the newsvendor and portfolio optimization problems.

title: Real-Time Solution of Quadratic Optimization Problems with Banded Matrices and Indicator Variables
authors: Andres Gomez; Shaoning Han; Leonardo Lozano
affiliations: University of Southern California, Los Angeles, California, 90089, United States; University of Southern California, The Daniel J. Epstein Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering, Los Angeles, California, 90089-0001, United States; University of Cincinnati, Cincinnati, Ohio, United States
abstract: We consider mixed-integer quadratic optimization problems with banded matrices and indicator variables. These problems arise pervasively in statistical inference problems with time-series data, where the banded matrix captures the temporal relationship of the underlying process. In particular, the problem studied arises in monitoring problems, where the decision-maker wants to detect changes or anomalies. We propose to solve these problems using decision diagrams. In particular we show how to exploit the temporal dependencies to construct exact and approximate decision diagrams. For problems over matrices with bandwidth equal to one, the proposed method runs in polynomial time. Moreover, if the bandwidth and condition number of the matrix is fixed, then we show that the proposed method can be modified to run into an additive approximation scheme. We also describe how to construct the convex hull of the set under study from the decision diagrams, and how to deploy the method online to solve the problems via a shortest path algorithm. Computational experiments show that, for problems with bandwidths less or equal than three, our proposed algorithm compares favorably to a state-of-the-art off-the-shelf solver in the offline setting, and that we are able to solve problems in milliseconds for the online setting.

title: On the Maximization of Long-Run Conditional Value-at-Risk for Markov Decision Processes
authors: Li Xia; Zhihui Yu; Haoran Wu
affiliations: School of Business, Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou 510275, China
abstract: Optimizing Risk-Seeking Sequential Decisions via Conditional Value-at-Risk Decision makers may exhibit risk-seeking preferences in finance, energy operations, and stochastic resource management, yet corresponding Markov decision process (MDP) theories remain underdeveloped. In this paper, “On the Maximization of Long-Run CVaR for Markov Decision Processes,” Xia, Yu, and Wu investigate infinite-horizon MDPs maximizing long-run conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) for instantaneous rewards. They prove optimality for stationary randomized policies and show deterministic policies may fail; an optimal policy randomizes over at most two actions. By converting the original problem into a minimax saddle point formulation, the authors develop solvable linear programming and globally convergent gradient descent algorithms. Results are further extended to joint mean-CVaR optimization and validated on real-world microgrid scheduling data. This work fills gaps for risk-seeking MDPs and delivers practical computation tools for tail-oriented sequential decision making.

title: Online Allocation with Heterogeneous Supply and Minimum Workload Guarantees
authors: Garud Iyengar; Raghav Singal
affiliations: Department of IEOR, Columbia University, New York, New York 10027; Tuck School of Business, Dartmouth College, Hanover, New Hampshire 03755
abstract: Keeping Gig Workers Working How should platforms allocate jobs when workers need a minimum amount of work to stay engaged? In their accepted paper, “Online Allocation with Heterogeneous Supply and Minimum Workload Guarantees,” Garud Iyengar and Raghav Singal study this question in online labor marketplaces, where workers differ in quality, capacity, and desired workload. The authors show that intuitive allocation rules can perform poorly. A first-come-first-served policy can favor lower-quality workers, whereas a quality-based greedy policy can cause high-capacity workers to leave when their workload requirements are not met. They develop Tracker, an online policy that combines admission control with a simple target-tracking rule: Each worker is assigned a target workload, and arriving jobs are directed toward workers who are most under their targets. Despite the stochastic nature of demand, the authors establish that Tracker is optimal. Computational experiments calibrated to a real labor marketplace show substantial improvements in allocation quality relative to standard policies, while maintaining workers’ minimum workload guarantees.

title: Looking Under the Hood of Commodity Currency Predictability
authors: Alexandre Jeanneret; Valeri Sokolovski
affiliations: School of Banking and Finance, UNSW Business School, Kensington, New South Wales 2033, Australia; Alberta School of Business, University of Alberta, Edmonton AB T6G 2R3, Canada
abstract: This paper revisits the exchange rate predictability of commodity currencies through the lens of market efficiency. Focusing on currencies with strong contemporaneous exposure to commodity prices, we show that changes in country-specific commodity export or import prices predict exchange rate fluctuations both in sample and out of sample. We establish four empirical facts: (i) the sign of the predictive relationship runs counter to standard risk-based explanations; (ii) predictability is concentrated at short horizons; (iii) predictability is driven by a small set of thinly traded currencies; and (iv) even sophisticated speculative traders adjust positions sluggishly in response to commodity price shocks in these currencies. Together, these findings suggest that predictability arises from the slow incorporation of information in less actively traded currencies, which is likely due to liquidity and position-building constraints, rather than from compensation for risk. The results also clarify the sources of commodity-based predictability in carry trade returns. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07249 .

title: Bargaining and Contract Forms in Distribution Channels: Why Do Slotting Fees Arise and Linear Contracts Persist?
authors: Øystein Foros; Hans Jarle Kind; Greg Shaffer
affiliations: Norwegian School of Economics (NHH), 5045 Bergen, Norway; Norwegian School of Economics (NHH), 5045 Bergen, Norway; and CESifo, 81679 Munich, Germany; University of Rochester, Rochester, New York 14627
abstract: Two empirical patterns emerge in business-to-business settings, particularly in retail distribution channels such as grocery markets. First, linear contracts are widely observed alongside nonlinear contracts with fixed payments, despite the claimed efficiency advantages of the latter. Second, when fixed payments arise, they often flow from suppliers to retailers (slotting fees) rather than the reverse. We develop and analyze a model of multilateral bargaining in which a supplier negotiates separately with competing retailers to explain these patterns. The key mechanism is a trade-off between two distortions: under linear contracts, wholesale prices reflect bargaining power and can be either above or below the channel-profit-maximizing level, whereas under two-part tariffs, wholesale prices are set to maximize bilateral surplus independently of bargaining power but are systematically too low from an overall channel perspective because of rent shifting across relationships. As a result, neither contractual form uniformly dominates; instead, relative performance depends on how bargaining shapes gains from trade across firms. When bargaining leads to slotting fees, two-part tariffs yield higher channel profits than linear contracts, whereas when it would imply payments from retailers to suppliers, linear contracts may perform better. These findings offer a unified explanation for the persistence of linear contracts alongside two-part tariffs, the direction of fixed payments, and the conditions under which each contractual form is likely to arise. This paper was accepted by Miguel Villas-Boas, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03426 .

title: “Generate” the Future of Work through AI: Empirical Evidence from Online Labor Markets
authors: Jin Liu; Xingchen Xu; Xi Nan; Yongjun Li; Yong Tan
affiliations: University of Science and Technology of China School of Management, Department of Management Science, Hefei, Anhui, China; University of Washington, Information Systems and Operations Management, Seattle, Washington, 98195-0005, United States; University of Washington, Michael G. Foster School of Business, Seattle, Washington, 98195, United States; USTC, management science, Hefei, 230026, China; University of Washington, Michael G. Foster School of Business, Seattle, Washington, 98195-3200, United States
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based generative AI systems are general-purpose tools capable of augmenting or even automating a wide range of job functions, positioning them to reshape labor market dynamics. However, predicting their precise impact a priori is challenging, given AI’s simultaneous effects on both demand and supply, as well as the strategic responses of market participants. Leveraging an extensive dataset from a leading online labor platform, we document a pronounced displacement effect and an overall contraction in submarkets where required skills closely align with core LLM functionalities. Although demand and supply both decline, the reduction in supply is comparatively smaller, thereby intensifying competition among freelancers. Notably, further analysis shows that this heightened competition is especially pronounced in programming-intensive submarkets. This pattern is attributed to skill-transition effects: by lowering the human-capital barrier to programming, ChatGPT enables incumbent freelancers to enter programming tasks. Moreover, these transitions are not homogeneous, with high-skilled freelancers contributing disproportionately to the shift. Our findings illuminate the multifaceted impacts of general-purpose AI on labor markets, highlighting not only the displacement of certain occupations but also the inducement of skill transitions within the labor supply. These insights offer practical implications for policymakers, platform operators, and workers.

title: Campaigns That Click: Unleashing the Power of Push Notifications on Mobile Apps
authors: Zhuping Liu; Bicheng Yang; Subodha Kumar
affiliations: Baruch College Zicklin School of Business, Marketing and International Business, New York, New York, United States; The Hong Kong Polytechnic University Faculty of Business, management and marketing, Hong Kong, Hong Kong; Temple University, Supply Chain, Information Systems, Marketing, and Statistics, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States
abstract: As mobile apps increasingly mediate digital engagement, push notifications have emerged as a key tool for directing user attention, yet systematic evidence on their behavioral and ecosystem-level effects remains limited. Using data from over 200 push campaigns and 60 million user-campaign observations on a leading U.S. mobile-offer marketplace, we combine large-scale observational analyses with controlled experiments to study how push notifications shape user engagement. We find that push notifications significantly increase same-day click-throughs to advertised merchants, with substantial heterogeneity across merchant characteristics, user characteristics, message design, and delivery timing. Beyond focal-merchant responses, notifications are associated with increased engagement with non-advertised merchants both within and across categories, suggesting that push notifications reshape attention across the marketplace ecosystem. Both the large-scale empirical analysis and controlled experiments yield evidence consistent with two complementary mechanisms—content-driven processing of notification information and reminder-based attention activation. The results also identify attentional saturation as a key boundary condition—repeated exposure produces diminishing responsiveness and may even reduce engagement at high notification frequencies. These findings position push notifications as a mobile-native attention-allocation lever that platforms can strategically deploy, while underscoring the need to balance engagement gains against user fatigue and attention costs.

title: Mobile Location-based Recommendation Systems and Local Businesses: Evidence from the Restaurant Industry
authors: Jin Soo Han; Gunwoong Lee; Keongtae Kim
affiliations: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology College of Business, IT Management, Seoul, Korea (the Republic of); Korea University, Management Information Systems, Seongbuk-gu, Seoul, Korea (the Republic of); Chinese University of Hong Kong, Decisions, Operations and Technology, Shatin, Hong Kong
abstract: We investigate the impact of mobile location-based recommendation systems (MLBRS) on the performance of local businesses. Leveraging a comprehensive dataset of 16,720 restaurants and quasi-experimental variation generated by the official launch of a leading MLBRS, we employ a 2-Stage Least Squares instrumental-variable framework to estimate the effect of algorithmic exposure on consumer engagement. Our analysis reveals that a 1% increase in exposure is associated with a 0.078% increase in clicks; separately, a 1% increase in clicks is associated with a 0.053% increase in visit intentions. Importantly, the estimated exposure effect is larger for geographically disadvantaged restaurants, but primarily at the discovery stage (clicks). This pattern highlights a boundary condition of MLBRS: algorithmic visibility can aid, but it does not by itself resolve the uncertainty involved in acting on a recommendation. Downstream conversion is stronger when restaurants provide richer digital information and reputation signals, including consumer reviews and owner-curated information such as photos and menus. Auxiliary credit-card sales data from a restricted Seoul subsample provide consistent evidence of a positive association between algorithmic exposure and revenue, suggesting that MLBRS can shape the connection of online recommendations to offline economic outcomes.

title: Risk Assessment of an Illegal Laboratory in Reedley, California, Using Geospatial Analysis of Open‐Source Epidemic Intelligence Data
authors: Atalay Goshu Muluneh; Rebecca Dawson; Jared Edgeworth; Natalie L. Cain; Ashley Quigly; Aye Moa; Samsung Lim; Chandini Raina MacIntyre
affiliations: Biosecurity Program, The Kirby Institute, Faculty of Medicine and Health the University of New South Wales Sydney Australia; Victorian Infectious Diseases Reference Laboratory Royal Melbourne Hospital, Doherty Institute for Infection and Immunity Melbourne Australia; School of Civil and Environmental Engineering University of New South Wales Sydney Australia; College of Public Service & Community Solutions and College of Health Solutions Arizona State University Tempe United States
abstract: ABSTRACT An illegal laboratory discovered in Reedley, California, in December 2022 was in a warehouse, operating without a license, handling about a thousand transgenic mice, chemicals, and possibly over 20 pathogens, including vials labeled Ebola, which were never tested but destroyed. This study aimed to estimate epidemic signals around the Reedley illegal laboratory using open‐source epidemic intelligence data. We utilized data from EPIWATCH, from October 2021 to October 2023, a year prior to and a year after the establishment of the illegal laboratory. The spatial pattern of outbreak signals was analyzed using hotspot analysis, and the distances of outbreak signals from the laboratory were measured. In California, an upward trend in outbreak signals of pathogens associated with the laboratory was noted in December 2022, April 2023, and August 2023. In the hotspot analysis, California and eight other states in the United States (US) were identified as hotspots. Narrative evidence revealed the presence of a sick employee working in the laboratory, whose child also became ill. Changes in disease patterns reported in California or the US in the year following the establishment of the illegal laboratory may or may not be linked to the illegal laboratory. A subsequent illegal lab linked to Reedley was identified in Las Vegas in 2026, highlighting the ongoing threat to biosecurity. EPIWATCH geospatial and temporal analysis can enhance the public health risk assessment of threats associated with illegal laboratories, especially when there is no available testing or reporting.

title: Issue Information
An Integrated Risk‐Informed Optimization Framework for Disinformation Interdiction in Coupled Information‐Physical Networks
authors: Daniel Cabrera Giraldo; Andrés D. González; Kash Barker
affiliations: School of Industrial and Systems Engineering University of Oklahoma Norman Oklahoma USA
abstract: ABSTRACT The manner in which society consumes and responds to information has significantly evolved in recent years, increasing the potential risk of interacting with, reacting to, and spreading misinformation and disinformation. In this paper, we introduce a novel integrated optimization framework that simultaneously models the dynamics of an information layer (where correct information or false information spreads) and a physical layer (where users interact with a physical infrastructure system). We consider an over‐the‐horizon problem in which an adversary seeks to disrupt physical infrastructure by spreading false information about its operation and performance, prompting users to behave in ways that degrade system performance. Focusing on public transit, we study how disinformation about station closures alters user behavior and system efficiency, and develop an optimization model to identify effective interdiction strategies that mitigate these impacts. The information layer incorporates personality‐driven susceptibility and simulates dis/information diffusion, while the physical layer uses a multicommodity network flow model to capture user movements and expose the effects of disinformation on travel time. Our integrated approach enables the joint analysis of both layers, revealing complex interdependencies that are overlooked when studied separately. A case study of the New York City subway system shows that even limited protective interventions can significantly reduce travel delays. In contrast, unmitigated disinformation can substantially degrade system performance. This research highlights the importance of integrated optimization‐based strategies for enhancing the resilience of transportation systems to information‐based threats and provides a foundation for future studies on dynamic disinformation influence on physical infrastructure systems.

title: EXPRESS: Do You Lose When You Sell Loose? Impact of Unpackaged Sales on Profit and Waste
authors: Ismail Kirci; Dorothee Honhon; Alp Muharremoglu
abstract: Loose sales — the sale of unpackaged products by unit or weight — are frequently promoted as a way to reduce waste because they allow consumers to purchase exactly the quantity they want, rather than being constrained by the fixed quantities dictated by the pre-packaged format. We study a retailer selling a highly perishable product under two possible formats: fixed-size packages and/or loose. The retailer chooses prices and package size to maximize profit. Consumers perceive loose products as fresher, but they also incur an inconvenience cost arising from the additional time and effort required. For the retailer, loose sales carry a higher unit variable cost due to increased labor requirements. In a homogeneous market, we show that, if consumers place substantially higher value on the loose option and its cost is not significantly greater than that of packaged sale, the retailer can make more profit selling only loose at a high price to consumers who buy the quantity they desire. Otherwise, the retailer is better off selling packages of large size, forcing consumers to buy more than they desire to purchase. Interestingly, consumer waste can actually be greater when the product is sold exclusively in loose format. In a heterogeneous market with two consumer segments which differ in the magnitude of their consumption needs, three possible optimal strategies emerge: selling only loose to both segments, selling only (relatively small) packages to both segments, or selling (relatively large) packages to high-consumption needs consumers and selling loose to the low-consumption needs consumers. Our results also demonstrate that selling loose instead of or alongside packages can often be a win-win strategy, simultaneously boosting retailer profits and reducing consumer waste compared to selling only packages. However, in some cases, introducing loose sales may increase waste. These findings indicate that retailers may derive financial gains from offering products in loose form; however, they should ensure that the associated sustainability benefits are genuine before positioning it as a green strategy. Likewise, policymakers seeking to reduce food waste should carefully consider product- and market-specific conditions rather than promoting loose sales as a universally effective waste-reduction measure.

title: EXPRESS: Interoperability Meets Accountability: How Data Interoperability and Experiential Quality Influence Malpractice Lawsuits
authors: Sukrit Pal; David E. Cantor; Anand Nair
abstract: A persistent challenge that many patients continue to face is substandard care including errors in their medical records (Sharma et al., 2019). To address this situation, health information exchanges (HIE) have been established to seamlessly share patient data across organizations. In this study, we examine whether policy-driven support for data interoperability—operationalized through health information exchange (HIE) systems—is associated with increased malpractice liability. Drawing on the empowerment literature, we argue that greater operational transparency enabled by data sharing may empower patients to scrutinize care quality, thereby elevating the risk of litigation. Using an eight-year panel data set covering 952 U.S. hospitals from 2010 to 2017 and over 24,000 malpractice case filings, we find that HIE adoption is associated with a statistically significant 10.5% increase in malpractice lawsuits. However, this effect is moderated by hospitals’ experiential quality, as measured by patient-reported experiences of communication, empathy, and responsiveness. In hospitals with high experiential quality, the effect of HIE adoption on malpractice lawsuits is reduced by 20.4%, suggesting that positive patient interactions can reduce the legal risks associated with HIE adoption. Our findings highlight a critical trade-off. While data interoperability improves operational coordination and patient engagement, it can also elevate legal exposure. This research contributes to the operations management and public policy literature by reframing interoperability not just as a backend coordination tool but also as a patient-facing technological development with reputational and legal implications.

title: EXPRESS: From Chit-Chat to Conversion: Cost-Efficient Conversational Recommendation via Retrospective Learning and Isolated Reflection
authors: Jiahui Wang; Hongke Zhao; Likang Wu; Bing Lv; Ning Jia
abstract: Conversational recommendation systems help digital platforms elicit user preferences through multi-turn interaction, but they often face a practical tension between recommendation accuracy and interaction cost when users provide vague or low-information inputs. This study follows a design science approach to develop a cost-conscious conversational recommendation artifact for such ambiguous service encounters. The artifact is guided by two design principles. First, retrospective outcome-guided supervision uses successful historical conversion trajectories as downstream anchors for improving responses at earlier low-information states. Second, isolated reflection separates recommendation generation from consistency checking, enabling diagnostic regeneration when candidate responses conflict with previously stated user constraints. In implementation, the artifact instantiates these principles through parameter-efficient adaptation of open-source large language models and prompt-isolated role switching over a shared backbone model. We validate the artifact on three conversational recommendation datasets covering movie and e-commerce settings, using outcome efficacy, interaction efficiency, process analysis, ablation analysis, robustness checks, and human evaluation. Here, interaction efficiency refers to user-visible dialogue turns, while computational burden is reported separately through training, memory, and latency measurements. The empirical results show that the artifact improves recommendation effectiveness while maintaining a favorable balance between interaction burden and conversion outcomes under the tested conditions. Process-level analysis further characterizes how recommendation behavior evolves over the course of dialogue. This study contributes transferable design principles for embedding retrospective preference optimization and isolated reflection into conversational recommendation systems, offering operational guidance for platforms seeking to improve personalization under constraints on interaction cost.

title: EXPRESS: When Good Practices Go Too Far: Overshooting in Organizational Culture
authors: Francisco Brahm; Christoph Loch; Joaquin Poblete
abstract: Business research has examined how useful practices can be made to spread and develop in organizations. However, practices have been observed “overshooting”: either over-diffusing—too many employees adopt them, including some whose usage is unproductive; or becoming over-sophisticated—the practice becomes too elaborate, reducing organizational performance. Independent models of over-diffusion and over-sophistication have been proposed; this paper integrates both aspects in a simple, unified model of overshooting. We offer a cultural evolution model that studies how interaction dynamics among employees are able to diffuse and stabilize an equilibrium of underperforming cultural practices, at the same time over-developing the practice so its sophistication goes beyond productive levels. People adopt practices from others based on information about the practice’s productive value, but also influenced by social dynamics with other employees, such as status. Our model clarifies the circumstances in which over-diffusion and over-sophistication can arise, and how these two elements of overshooting relate to each other. We map our model in detail to two cases---process management practices (e.g., six sigma) and Uber's aggressive culture---and discuss the managerial implications.

title: EXPRESS: Participation Governance in Consumer and AI Co-creation: Whether to Intervene and How to Design It
authors: Mengxia Zhang; Brian Rongqing Han; Tianshu Sun; Lan Luo; Joseph M. Golden
abstract: Artificial intelligence reshapes digital mass customization by altering the structure of consumer co-creation. When consumers start from a draft generated by artificial intelligence rather than a blank canvas, outcomes are jointly determined by two stages: whether consumers initiate co-creation and, conditional on participation, how much refinement effort they exert. This separation makes participation a governable design margin—an issue that is largely muted in traditional blank-canvas customization, where participation and effort are tightly bundled. Partnering with a leading United States online retailer of personalized photo products, we study whether and how firm interventions at the participation stage shape downstream purchase outcomes. We develop a two-stage model in which, relative to a baseline with organic participation, a nudge lowers start-up frictions and expands voluntary entry, whereas a mandate serves as a strong boundary-case intervention that guarantees entry but can weaken how participation translates into purchase, generating a reach–efficiency trade-off. We examine these predictions in two randomized experiments. In Study 1, a light-touch nudge increases participation by 5.98 percentage points and raises revenue and order frequency. The evidence is consistent with gains arising primarily through expanded entry into consumer co-creation with artificial intelligence. In Study 2, mandates increase participation relative to nudges, but we find no clear evidence of additional gains in purchase or revisit intentions. Instead, mandates increase low-value participation, in which consumers exert minimal effort and report low purchase intention. Together, these findings show that in mass customization enabled by artificial intelligence, participation governance is a consequential design choice: firms must consider not only how many consumers initiate co-creation, but also whether the participation they induce creates downstream value.

title: EXPRESS: Harnessing Renewable Portfolio Standards for Sustainable Futures: An Empirical Examination of Spillover Effects
authors: Chunjie Zhao; Anqi Wu; Ramanathan Subramanyam
abstract: Given the importance of managing industrial energy consumption, setting standards and implementing policies that encourage renewable energy use is crucial for incentivizing sustainable firm practices. Public policy designs must align closely with firms’ environmental policies to help mitigate greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and support a sustainable future. While research on policy impacts on firm environmental performance and the supply chain's role in sustainability is growing, a critical, understudied effect is the spillover of government rules to supply chain partners and peer firms, especially those outside the direct purview of environmental regulations. This paper presents a novel approach that integrates data from the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) and the Renewable Portfolio Standards (RPS). The latter refers to state-driven initiatives that incentivize electricity consumption from eligible renewable resources. We examine the causal effects of state-level policies on firm-level GHG emission intensity, with particular emphasis on the spillover effects of policies on unregulated firms across markets. We break down emission intensity into Scope 1 and Scope 2 and capture facility-level data to analyze spillover effects in granular detail. Using a staggered difference-in-differences methodology, our analysis finds a promising negative association between RPS introduction and GHG emission intensity among unregulated firms across industries. Interestingly, firms headquartered in states with more conservative initial targets during RPS adoption and progressive, milestone-based implementation strategies have significantly lower GHG emission intensity than those headquartered in states with more aggressive initial targets or long-term absolute targets. Our findings have significant implications for developing environmental regulations and public policies aimed at reducing GHG emission intensity.

title: EXPRESS: What Drives Physician Efficiency? Evidence from Emergency Department Operations
authors: Raha Imanirad; Soroush Saghafian; Stephen J. Traub; Nicole R. Hodgson
abstract: Emergency department (ED) physicians play a critical role in healthcare, serving on the frontline of acute care delivery. Yet increasing demand, resource constraints, and growing patient complexity pose significant challenges to physician efficiency. In this study, we investigate the determinants of ED physician efficiency using a multi-stage framework. First, we apply Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) to measure individual physician efficiency based on data from 110,325 patient visits at a leading U.S. hospital. Second, we use a Tobit regression model to analyze how physician experience, shift familiarity, and patient severity influence physician efficiency. Third, we conduct comprehensive robustness checks, including omitted variable bias sensitivity analyses, permutation tests, and machine learning-based classification analyses, to address concerns regarding endogeneity and potential model misspecification. Our results show that physician efficiency increases with experience at a diminishing rate. Efficiency also varies with shift familiarity, with the estimated association weakening as physician experience increases. In addition, higher patient severity is associated with lower physician efficiency, consistent with the greater resource demands of caring for more clinically complex patients. This negative association is attenuated for more experienced physicians, suggesting that experienced physicians are better able to maintain efficiency when managing more demanding clinical conditions. Our findings offer actionable recommendations for improving ED operations. Staffing strategies that assign relatively more experienced physicians to higher-severity patients may help maintain physician efficiency, while shift familiarity may inform a scheduling strategy that emphasizes greater scheduling consistency for relatively less experienced physicians and greater flexibility for relatively more experienced physicians. Simulation results further illustrate the potential reductions in physician resource use associated with these strategies. Together, these findings highlight the value of evidence-based physician staffing and scheduling to improve physician efficiency in EDs.

title: Leveraging digital capabilities for supply chain recovery and renewal: the mediating roles of spontaneous and creative improvisation
authors: Lei Wang; Chun Zhang
affiliations: Glorious Sun School of Economics and Management, Donghua University , ,; Grossman School of Business, University of Vermont , , ,
abstract: Purpose Building on the dynamic capability view (DCV) and supply chain (SC) literature on digitalization, improvisation and resilience, we examined how different digital capabilities influence different post-disruption SC resilience outcomes (recovery and renewal) through distinct forms of improvisation in cross-border SCs. Design/methodology/approach Our sample comprises 217 matched Chinese supplier–buyer dyads, with buyers located in 66 countries. Confirmatory factor analysis and multiple regression were used to test the measurement model and hypothesized relationships, respectively. Robustness and endogeneity tests were also performed. Findings We find that digital market orientation is positively associated with creative improvisation, while its relationship with spontaneous improvisation is non-significant. In contrast, digital process innovation is positively associated with spontaneous improvisation, while its relationship with creative improvisation is non-significant. Furthermore, spontaneous improvisation is positively associated with SC recovery, while creative improvisation is positively associated with SC renewal. Creative improvisation mediates the relationship between digital market orientation and SC renewal, while spontaneous improvisation mediates the relationship between digital process innovation and SC recovery. Originality/value This study reveals distinct paths through which different digital capabilities contribute to post-disruption SC resilience. By differentiating digital capabilities, improvisational capabilities, and resilience outcomes, the study extends DCV-based SC resilience research by explaining how the adaptive potential embedded in these digital capabilities is translated through distinct improvisational capabilities into post-disruption SC resilience outcomes in cross-border SCs.

title: How Peer Working Hours Shape Individual Preferences: Experimental Evidence From Germany
authors: Zarah Westrich
affiliations: Institute for Socio‐Economics, University of Duisburg‐Essen Duisburg Germany
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how colleagues' working hours influence individual working hours preferences. We conducted a representative survey experiment among German employees in 2024, in which participants received randomized information about colleagues' working hours. We combine the survey experiment with quantitative and LLM‐based text analysis of an open‐ended question. Colleagues' hours causally influence stated preferences, yet respondents' explanations focus on personal reasons. This shows that social factors influence working time preferences alongside the individual considerations that respondents most frequently identify. Our findings highlight the importance of collective action for working‐time policy and reveal methodological considerations for studying labor supply preferences.
journal: Industrial Relations: A Journal of Economy and Society

title: Follow the Money: The State and the Architecture of Union Funding
authors: Assaf S. Bondy
affiliations: Bristol Business School University of Bristol and Haifa University, Haifa. Bristol UK
abstract: ABSTRACT Trade unions need money to sustain the staff, infrastructure and activities on which all forms of union power depend, yet the financial dimensions of unions and their power have been largely overlooked in the comparative study of industrial relations. This article addresses the gap by using unions’ financial means as a revealing lens for understanding the role of the state in shaping union power. The comparison distinguished two ideal‐typical logics of state action behind union funding. Under indirect action, the state enables unions to convert membership into income, producing a tight coupling between union funds and organisational power. Under direct action, the state channels funds to unions on the basis of their recognised societal roles, decoupling income from membership. Systematised during the early decades of the twentieth century, these two action paths present fundamental transformations through liberalisation, leading to the financialisation and politicisation of union funding. By analysing the structures and changes in unions’ financial sustainability, this framework reveals the state's constitutive role in shaping and transforming union power.

title: Recomposing Management Education Under Climate Crisis: Towards a Composting Heuristic for Epistemic Change
authors: Ling Li; Kate Seymour; Rosalyn Marron; Helena Kettleborough; Catherine Brentnall; Olivia Tomlinson; Sarah Walker; Nor Yusup; John Lever
affiliations: Department of Strategy, Enterprise and Sustainability Manchester Metropolitan University All Saints, Oxford Road Manchester UK
abstract: Abstract Management learning and education (MLE) is increasingly critiqued for its reliance on anthropocentric and profit‐maximization paradigms, which fail to adequately address the escalating ecological and climate crises. In this article, we call for an epistemic shift in MLE by introducing the metaphor of composting as a lens for collective reflexive critique. We propose a composting heuristic inspired by the social practices of managing organic matter—landfill, industrial composting and community composting—to help MLE educators critically examine the epistemic foundations, limitations and possibilities that shape their teaching and learning practices. This metaphorical framework highlights an epistemic transition towards a multispecies and regenerative pedagogical paradigm, grounded in relational ontology, care and embodied practice. We argue that engaging with the metaphor of composting—and reflecting critically on one's positioning within the landfill‐industrial‐community composting heuristic—can catalyse a collective endeavour to drive epistemic change in MLE in response to the urgent demands of climate and ecological breakdown.

title: ‘I'm Not Smoking; I'm Just Vaping’: Deciphering the Reasons for and Against Vaping and Intention to Quit Among Young Consumers
authors: Hongfei Liu; Fahad Ibrahim; Fenfang Lin; Yuanming Qiu; Yuanyi Xu
affiliations: Southampton Business School University of Southampton Southampton UK; Birmingham Business School University of Birmingham Edgbaston UK; Newcastle University Business School Newcastle University Newcastle upon Tyne UK
abstract: Abstract Vaping has become a defining feature of youth culture and a fast‐expanding consumer practice, yet little is known about how young people rationalize their continued use despite awareness of health risks and social controversy. Drawing on behavioral reasoning theory (BRT) and insights from social identity theory (SIT), this study examines how young consumers construct, compare and prioritize reasons for and against vaping under conditions of uncertainty, thereby deciphering their intention to quit. Using a mixed‐methods design, it combines 21 in‐depth interviews with a survey of 804 young adult vapers in the UK. The findings indicate that conspiracy beliefs, scepticism and perceived uncountability are positively associated with relative disadvantage, which in turn predicts ambivalence and subsequently intention to quit. Ambivalence, in turn, is linked with stronger intention to quit, particularly among individuals with a strong future time perspective, whereas fear of social exclusion appears to weaken the effect of relative disadvantage on ambivalence. The study advances BRT by using evaluability as a conceptual lens to explain why certain reasons become more salient. By integrating cognitive reasoning with social identity, it offers theoretical and policy insights for enhancing health communication and fostering more informed behavioural engagement among young consumers.

title:
“Borrowing intelligence to build a business”: The promise of open‐source
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    for entrepreneurship
authors: Georg von Krogh; Ann‐Kristin Weiser; Patrick Nicolas Tinguely
affiliations: Department of Management, Technology, and Economics ETH Zurich Zürich Switzerland
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) is an increasingly important yet poorly understood frontier for entrepreneurial activity. We identify four defining features that shape new ventures' engagement with OSAI communities: dependence on sponsoring firms, layered licensing regimes, regulatory risks, and nation‐state influence. We develop the OSAI Framework for Market Entry to explain how open‐weight models relocate, rather than merely lower, entry barriers across six domains in AI‐enabled product and service markets. They may reduce resource barriers but create dependence on the governance of borrowed components, shifting the binding constraint from technical to commercial entry and value capture through complementary assets. We discuss contributions to research on entrepreneurial entry and strategy, private‐collective innovation, the openness paradox, and the new venture life cycle, and outline directions for future research. Managerial Summary Open‐source artificial intelligence (OSAI) offers new ventures access to powerful resources for developing AI‐enabled products and services without building AI capabilities from scratch. Yet new ventures must often contend with four key governance dependencies that shape how they engage with OSAI communities: reliance on large technology firms that contribute and steer critical layers of the AI stack, licensing terms that vary by layer, emerging regulatory requirements, and growing nation‐state influence over OSAI. Our OSAI Framework for Market Entry identifies where OSAI can lower entry barriers, where constraints shift instead, and how new ventures can manage the trade‐offs resulting from governance dependencies. It helps new ventures and investors evaluate when, where, and how to build on OSAI components, and which complementary assets can protect their returns.

title: Concentration and convergence: Regional productivity in Türkiye, 1950–2020
authors: Ulaş Karakoç
affiliations: Department of Economics Kadir Has University Cibali İstanbul Turkey
abstract: Abstract This paper presents a comprehensive long‐run analysis of regional productivity convergence in Türkiye using a novel dataset combining newly compiled employment estimates with recent output estimates. The seven‐decade analysis reveals substantial productivity convergence driven by labour reallocation away from agriculture alongside within‐industry convergence. A distinctive pattern emerges: aggregate economic concentration proceeded together with productivity convergence, with distinct regional clusters forming. Furthermore, shift‐share decomposition shows industry‐mix effects persistently explain significant regional productivity variation, reflecting sustained agriculture‐other sectors productivity differences, with western regions enjoying both favourable sectoral composition and regional competitiveness advantages. From a policy perspective, agricultural productivity improvements offer significant potential for reducing regional disparities.

title: The Rise of Alternatives
authors: Juliane Begenau; Pauline Liang; Emil Siriwardane
affiliations: Stanford GSB, NBER, and CEPR ,; Georgia Tech ,; Harvard Business School and NBER ,
abstract: Abstract Since the 2000s, U.S. public pension funds have actively shifted their risky investments away from public equities and toward alternative assets like private equity and hedge funds—some much more than others. We explore a range of possible explanations for these trends and argue that beliefs about the risk-adjusted return of alternatives have played a central role. Pension beliefs are shaped by investment consultants, peers, and experience in the 1990s. Other demand-side channels related to risk-seeking motives, spending needs, and fund governance have weaker empirical support. We also consider supply-side factors and agency interpretations of the data. (JEL G11, G23, G41, H75)

title: The Economics of Data Unions: Optimal Data Sharing and Coordination
authors: Lin William Cong; Simon Mayer
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University, ABFER, and NBER; Carnegie Mellon University , Tepper School of Business
abstract: Abstract We develop a model of data-driven competition in which product quality depends on users’ data contributions and firms’ investments in data infrastructure. Users’ inability to internalize the value generated by their data, together with firms’ strategic investment incentives, can lead to data underinvestment—limiting quality—or overinvestment—concentrating market power. We introduce a data union that coordinates users’ contributions and can be implemented through a data trust or intermediary that aggregates user data. By shaping data compensation, the union enables users to capture and internalize more of their data’s value, enhancing user welfare, especially when combined with data sharing among firms. We apply these insights to financial data, digital payments, and Open Finance. Our analysis shows that data portability can strengthen competition but, without coordination, may leave data investment too low or excessive.

title: Corporate Tax Changes and Credit Costs
authors: Yota D. Deli; Manthos D. Delis; Iftekhar Hasan; Panagiotis N. Politsidis; Anthony Saunders
abstract: Abstract We examine changes in the state corporate tax rate across the U.S. and their implications on the pricing and quantity of loans. We find that the cost of credit decreases by approximately 10 basis points following a tax cut. When we account for the magnitude of tax changes, a one‐percentage‐point tax cut (hike) is associated with a 10.5 (9.2) basis‐point decrease (increase) in loan spreads. Our findings mainly originate from the demand side: large firms are able to mitigate the effects of tax increases, while less profitable firms experience larger reductions in borrowing costs following tax cuts. The effect on the equilibrium loan amount is statistically and economically insignificant, consistent with a weak supply effect and an inelastic loan supply curve.

title: Measurement Error, Manipulation, and the Value of Short‐Term Performance in Job Retention
authors: Naomi Rothenberg
affiliations: Department of Accounting and Business Analytics University of Alberta Edmonton Alberta Canada
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies how the accuracy of a short‐term performance measure affects its value when a principal decides whether to retain or fire an agent, who can manipulate that measure. Compared with ignoring performance and never firing the agent, the performance measure is valuable when the savings in the expected cost of the retention error is more than the expected cost of the firing error. A more accurate performance measure can have a non‐monotonic effect on its value: Greater accuracy improves the principal's ability to correctly identify the agent, which increases efficient firing, but it causes the incompetent agent to increase manipulation to avoid being fired, which increases inefficient retention. With a less accurate performance measure, the incompetent agent has weaker incentives for manipulation, and an increase in accuracy increases its value due to the identification effect. With a more accurate performance measure, the manipulation effect dominates, and an increase in accuracy decreases its value. The results imply that the principal prefers an imperfect performance measure when the agent can choose the level of manipulation.

title: Religion and early fertility in the United States: changes during the second demographic transition
authors: Jeremy E Uecker; Riley S Peterson
affiliations: Department of Sociology, Baylor University, United States
abstract: Abstract We assess how changes in early fertility varied among US women with different religious characteristics, and how the associations between religion and early fertility changed across birth cohorts from 1950 to 1993. Using data from the National Survey of Family Growth, we examine the timing of nonmarital, marital, and overall first births through age 24. Results from life tables and discrete-time event history models reveal that increases in early nonmarital first births were smaller among women who attended religious services more frequently in childhood, whereas early marital births declined at similar rates irrespective of childhood religious service attendance. Because early births became increasingly nonmarital across birth cohorts, women who attended religious services more frequently in childhood became less likely to have an early birth overall. Early fertility differences by religious tradition generally converged across cohorts, although women raised conservative Protestant continued to have higher likelihoods of early birth relative to women raised in other religious traditions net of controls. Women who were raised nonreligious remained similar to conservative Protestants in their likelihood of nonmarital childbearing across cohorts and became statistically similar to them in their overall early births in the latest cohort. Changes in early fertility during the second demographic transition therefore varied by religious background and reshaped the relationship between religion and early fertility.

title: Learning traps
authors: Hassan Sayed
affiliations: Market Shaping Accelerator Center for Global Development, Washington DC USA
abstract: Abstract When constituents are uncertain about whether leaders' policy preferences align with their interests, policy choices generate a trade‐off between payoffs and information. Leaders can experiment with their preferred policy, but if the outcome is bad, constituents learn this and threaten office removal. I use a repeated model of political agency to analyze how this trade‐off shapes long‐lived, term‐unlimited leaders' policy choices. When there is uncertainty about the optimal policy for constituents, leaders implement “learning traps”: spatially intermediate policies that halt learning about what the best policy is. They experiment only when their preferences are very likely to be aligned with constituents, a contrast to the “gambling for resurrection” logic ubiquitous in the literature. I provide a case study that examines how the 1861 reforms ending Serfdom in Imperial Russia represented the logic of a “learning trap” and illustrate additional applications of the model to political contagion and economic policymaking.
